similar_scenes.name: Segunda invasión británica y MTV
similar_scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
similar_scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
similar_scenes.desc: En 1982 el new pop deja de ser un sueño de periodistas: «Don't You Want Me», «Tainted Love» y «The Look of Love» anuncian una nueva invasión, y en 1983 la segunda camada (Duran Duran, Culture Club, Wham!, Eurythmics, Thompson Twins) conquista Estados Unidos gracias a MTV, canal ideado por Michael Nesmith que, sin vídeos americanos, dependía de los británicos, más videogénicos y cultivados en el estilo («I want my MTV»). A Flock of Seagulls, Altered Images («Happy Birthday»), Simple Minds («Promised You a Miracle», New Gold Dream), Haircut 100, Kajagoogoo; Bowie se broncea con «Let's Dance». El new pop reexporta música negra (Chic, P-Funk, Quincy Jones) a la América blanca. En el Reino Unido, 1983 se vive en cambio como un año infausto: reelección de Thatcher, «Kill Ugly Pop» en las paredes y la vuelta de la conciencia social.

podcast.title: Cultural Storm Timeline (1991-1997)
podcast.body: Britpop is described as a "perfect cultural storm" that ran from about 1991 to 1997, following a six-year cycle including a build-up, a frenzy peak (12-18 months), and a long, slow decline. During this era, "London was swinging again" and British acts sold "tens of millions of albums." "This party ran from about 1991 to 1997."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 4: Britpop

podcast.title: British Market Receptiveness (1993)
podcast.body: In 1993, the British music market was experiencing a powerful surge, creating an exceptionally receptive environment for new bands. This strong momentum, fueled by existing acts like Blur and Suede, was a critical factor in the rapid and successful emergence of groups like Oasis. "El mercado musical británico como a final de 1993 era ser evidente, me refiero con Blur, con suade, con muchas cosas que ya estaban embujando muy fuerte."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: OASIS: Pilares del Brit Pop

podcast.title: Official Start (April 1993)
podcast.body: Some British texts and articles suggest that the Britpop movement officially began with Suede's cover story in SELECT magazine in April 1993, coinciding with the release of their debut album. "el ripop empiezo oficialmente con la portada de abril de 1993 en la revista SELECT."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: SUEDE: Pilares del Brit Pop

podcast.title: Britpop's Expanding Roster (1994-1995)
podcast.body: Beyond Blur, Oasis, and Suede, the British music media actively sought out and promoted other "homegrown candidates for superstardom," with Elastica becoming a key target, fueled by frontwoman Justine Frischmann's past in Suede and relationship with Damon Albarn. "the British music media felt duty-bound to uncover and annoyed more candidates for homegrown superstardom."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Coined Term from The Face - May 1994
podcast.body: The term "Britpop" originated from "the B word," an abbreviation for British pop, published by The Face magazine in May 1994. By the end of 1994, the term was widely adopted for numerous "unabashedly British" bands. "Then a magazine called The Face published the B word in May of 1994 as an abbreviation of British pop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Peak Years - 1994-1996
podcast.body: The period from 1994 through 1996 represented the peak years for Britpop, characterized by a resurgence of British pride, homegrown talent, and songs reminiscent of classic British acts like The Beatles and The Stones. "1994 through to 1996 were the peak years for Brit Pop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Decline Factors (Late 1995-1997)
podcast.body: The genre began to get "wobbly" due to a loss of focus with too many mediocre bands, criminal overexposure of its stars, the pressure for follow-up albums to *Parklife* and *Morning Glory*, and rampant drug use (heroin and cocaine) taking its toll on musicians and the industry. "First of all, everybody was starting to lose focus."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 4: Britpop

podcast.title: Golden Age (1995)
podcast.body: The Britpop movement reached its full peak and golden age around 1995, marked by significant album releases like Blur's "Parklife" (April 1994) and Oasis's "(What's the Story) Morning Glory?" (August 1995), which propelled the movement to its highest point of popularity and influence.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: BLUR: Pilares del Brit Pop

podcast.title: Peak and Inevitable Decline - Summer 1995
podcast.body: Britpop reached its peak in the summer of 1995, followed by an "inevitable decline." The momentum initially masked the cracks, but signs like BBC Radio 1's policy shift and the University of Leeds symposium on Britpop reflected its widespread influence before the downturn. "The peak of Britpop was the summer of 1995. After that came the long, slow, inevitable decline."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Peak and Media Frenzy (Summer 1995)
podcast.body: Britpop reached its peak in the summer of 1995, characterized by non-stop media coverage across print, radio, and TV, widespread paparazzi and gossip, and even a *Vanity Fair* feature on "Cool Britannia and Swing in London." "The party reached its peak in the summer of 1995."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Peak and Overexposure (Mid-1995)
podcast.body: The Britpop party started to peak in the summer of 1995, fueled by rivalries like the Blur vs. Oasis chart war. However, it also suffered from overexposure, with every indie label "throwing bands against the wall," and major players like Oasis constantly in the press, even detailing Noel Gallagher's wife's shopping sprees. "The party started to peak in the summer of 1995, and the best part was the war between blur and oasis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 4: Britpop

podcast.title: Post-Peak Decline (Late 1995)
podcast.body: After reaching its peak in 1995, particularly with the massive success of Oasis's *What's the Story (Morning Glory)?*, Britpop could "not possibly get any bigger," signaling that its trajectory was inevitably "down." "Britpop itself could not possibly get any bigger. So you know what that means, right? There was only one direction left to go. Down."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: The Great Battle of Britpop (1995)
podcast.body: The "Great Battle of Britpop," particularly highlighted by the simultaneous single releases of Oasis and Blur in 1995, was critically dismissed as a "discographic nonsense" or marketing ploy. Despite this, it became a significant cultural event, with Oasis ultimately "winning" in terms of sales and public recognition. "todo eso de la gran batería de ripop pero una patraña discográfica."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: OASIS: Pilares del Brit Pop

podcast.title: Wobbling and Decline (1995-1996)
podcast.body: As 1995 transitioned into 1996, Britpop began to show signs of instability and "getting a little wobbly," indicating the natural progression of a cultural storm reaching its end. "And as 1995 turned into 1996, it became apparent that Britpop was getting a little wobbly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Implosion and Abandonment (1996)
podcast.body: At its peak in 1996, Britpop abruptly imploded and rapidly disappeared from the media. This demise was largely due to the major record companies abandoning the movement when it was at its highest point, seeking new market trends. "en pleno auge de 1996, cuando estál nos dio un disco de Blurba Oasis, cuando había salido el combi de suéd, cuando había salido el different class, de repente el beat-pop casi imploció una idea desaparece, empiezó una muerte muy rápida en la que desaparece de los medios."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El BRIT POP como negocio discográfico

podcast.title: Reason for OMD's Retirement (1996)
podcast.body: In 1996, the popularity of Britpop among younger audiences contributed to Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark's decision to gracefully retire, as their 80s synthesizer sound no longer resonated with the current trends. "The kids were all about Britpop and a synthesizer band from the 80s just didn't cut it anymore, so the group gracefully retired."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: "Dirty Word" by End of 1997
podcast.body: By the end of 1997, Britpop became "pretty much a dirty word" from which artists distanced themselves, as the original audience had grown up and moved on. This period was also marked by increased drug use, particularly heroin, which led to fragmentation. "And by the end of 1997, Britpop was pretty much a dirty word from which everyone distanced themselves."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Decline and End (Circa 1997)
podcast.body: The Britpop movement began to die around 1997. This period saw key bands like Blur starting to abandon the genre and pursue entirely different musical directions, signaling the end of Britpop's dominant era.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: BLUR: Pilares del Brit Pop

podcast.title: Decline of Britpop (1997)
podcast.body: By 1997, the Britpop genre was in sharp decline, with its purist form losing relevance. Many bands, including Pulp, were actively experimenting with new sounds like hardcore and lofi, while others were disbanding, making it a challenging period for acts rooted in traditional Britpop. "ya 1997, malamente era época para Britpop y menos aún para ese Britpop tan purista."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: OASIS: Pilares del Brit Pop

podcast.title: End of an Era (1997)
podcast.body: By the end of 1997, everyone was distancing themselves from Britpop, the party was over, and the public and media were bored. The wave had run its course, precisely around the predicted six-year mark, with the Spice Girls and "girl power" becoming the new cultural drivers. "By the time the year was over, everybody was distancing themselves from anything to do with Britpop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 4: Britpop

podcast.title: Official End (1997)
podcast.body: By the end of 1997, Britpop was "officially over," with most artists distancing themselves from the genre due to a "bad hangover," the toll of drug use, and public/media boredom. Its influence would live on, but the wave had passed, consistent with the typical six-year cycle of cultural storms. "By the time the year was over, almost everyone was distancing themselves from anything to do with Britpop. The party was officially over."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: "Hunger for Musical Novelties" (Early 90s)
podcast.body: The early 1990s in the United Kingdom experienced a significant "hunger for musical novelties," creating a fertile ground for new bands like Suede and Blur to emerge and gain rapid relevance even before releasing their first albums. This context contributed to the immense impact of Suede's debut. "había un grandísimo hambre de novedades musicales dentro del Reino Unido."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: SUEDE: Pilares del Brit Pop

podcast.title: 1990s Heroin Epidemic
podcast.body: A significant portion of the Britpop scene in the 1990s was heavily impacted by heroin use. "a vast swath of the Britpop scene of the 1990s"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: RockNRoll Drugs

podcast.title: 90s Music Scene
podcast.body: Britpop is mentioned as one of the diverse genres present in the 1990s music scene, alongside grunge, third wave ska, and others, indicating a rich and varied musical landscape for discovery.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What A Drag It Is Getting Old (Musically)

podcast.title: Absorbed "New Wave of New Wave"
podcast.body: The "new wave of new wave" movement, emerging in the early 1990s, was short-lived because many of the bands within it were eventually subsumed into the larger Britpop genre. "many of the bands tagged with that label were soon subsumed into something bigger that we call Brit Pop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave

podcast.title: Acknowledged 90s Genre
podcast.body: Britpop was mentioned as one of the significant genres already covered in the broader discussion of 90s music, indicating its prominent role alongside Grunge in defining the era's sound. "We've already covered several. Grunge and Britpop, of course."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 7: The Other Genres

podcast.title: Age Diversity
podcast.body: The Britpop scene is cited as an example of a musical style where artists often had a wider range of ages, such as Vimo Galman (19 years old) and Jarvis Cocker (in his thirties), in contrast to the more age-homogeneous Generation X protagonists of grunge. "muchas veces en los estilos pues se junta gente que tiene 19 años, alguna gente tiene 30, otra pues pensé por ejemplo en el ripop se estaba juntando gente como Vimo Galman que tenía 19 años con gente como Jarvis Coquer que tenía 30 y pico."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cuál fue el primer disco de Grunge?

podcast.title: All-Encompassing Social Phenomenon
podcast.body: At its peak, Britpop was an all-encompassing social phenomenon in the UK, fostering a renewed sense of pride across the island and making London the perceived "most swinging place on earth." "At its height, Brit Pop was an all-encompassing social phenomenon in the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Analogy for German Rock
podcast.body: The desire of young German musicians to create their own distinct identity, rather than imitating Anglo-American rock, is compared to how young British musicians in the early 1990s reacted to the "invasion" of Grunge from the US. Their resistance led to the emergence of Britpop as a uniquely British sound. "This is not unlike how many young British musicians felt in the early 1990s when Grunge was invading the UK. They had to fight back and the result was Britpop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Explaining Krautrock

podcast.title: Artist Fragmentation
podcast.body: By the late 1990s, Britpop artists were either "hung over from their party" or "messed up on drugs," with bands like Oasis flatlining and Blur turning their back on the genre. "If the Britpop kids weren't hung over from their party, they were messed up on drugs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 9: The Festivals

podcast.title: British Response to Grunge
podcast.body: Britpop emerged as the British music scene's homegrown response to the spread and dominance of American Grunge in the mid-1990s. "Britpop, which was their homegrown response to American Grunge"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 500th Show!

podcast.title: Britpop Era Overview
podcast.body: This era, running from approximately 1991 to 1997, saw London "swaying again" and British acts selling tens of millions of albums globally. It was characterized as fresh, fun, and cool, but eventually collapsed under "overexposure, boredom, and drugs." "That party ran from about 1991 to 1997."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Britpop – Direct Descendant of Madchester; British Musical Nationalism; Beatles, Stones, Kinks, Who, Glam
podcast.body: Britpop was the major UK genre of the 1990s, the direct descendant of the Madchester/Baggy sound, adding British musical nationalism — embracing the influences of the Beatles, the Stones, the Kinks, the Who, Glam, and the Mod era. Key bands included Blur, Suede, Supergrass, Pulp, Menswear, and — biggest of all — Oasis. "It took what madchester was all about and added in some British musical nationalism, embracing the influences of the Beatles and the Stones and the Kinks and the Who and the Glam era and the Mod era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: A Guide to Genres: Part 2

podcast.title: Britpop's Defensive Origin
podcast.body: Britpop emerged as a defensive response from the UK against the invasion of grunge from American bands, aiming to reassert British rock tradition which was being supplanted by acts like Pearl Jam, Nirvana, and Soundgarden. "From the very beginning, Britpop's goal was to defend the empire from the grunge marauders from the colonies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Britpop's Funkiest
podcast.body: The Stone Roses are highlighted as "the funkiest Britpop band of them all," indicating a unique rhythmic quality within the genre that blended rock with dance music influences. "Out of all the bands to come out of Britain in the late 1980s, no one was more popular and influential than the Stone Roses."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rhythm Sections

podcast.title: Celebration of Britishness
podcast.body: The Britpop era of the mid-1990s was characterized by its focus on "celebrating Britishness," which included acknowledging preceding British rock artists. "Elastica was one of the great bands of the Britpop era of the middle 90s. And Britpop was all about celebrating Britishness."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Unfortunate Sonic Coincidences

podcast.title: Characteristics of Britpop
podcast.body: Emerging in the mid-1990s, Britpop was a musical era characterized by the celebration of Britishness. This often involved acknowledging and paying homage to earlier British rock artists who had paved the way. "And Britpop was all about celebrating Britishness, this meant acknowledging those who came before to blaze a trail for British rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sonic Coincidences in Alt-Rock Part 1

podcast.title: Counterinsurgency Against Grunge
podcast.body: Britpop emerged as a direct "counterinsurgency" launched by the British against the rise of grunge and the alternative nation in North America, promoting homegrown talent and sounds. "This show is about the counterinsurgency that the British launched against that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Cultural Context
podcast.body: A musical era flourishing in the mid-1990s, characterized by its celebration of "British-ness" and a tendency for artists to acknowledge and draw inspiration from preceding British rock acts. "Britpop was all about celebrating British-ness. That meant acknowledging those who came before to blaze a trail for British rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Unfortunate Sonic Coincidences

podcast.title: Cultural Leadership in Toronto
podcast.body: The speaker recalled that before the internet took off around 1996, his radio station played a crucial role in disseminating information about British music, often weeks ahead of magazines. The station championed bands like Happy Mondays, Stone Roses, and The Charlatans, leading the culture in Toronto, Ontario, Western New York, and potentially beyond. "I think we led the culture in Toronto for sure, certainly in Ontario, certainly in Western New York and maybe beyond."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Cultural Movement
podcast.body: Britpop was a significant cultural and musical scene in the UK, exemplified by figures like Damon Albarn and Justine Frischmann being considered its "first couple." The genre also experienced a decline, leading to bands like Elastica struggling with album sales by the late 1990s. "Britpop had died off years earlier, the songs weren't there and sales were… well, dismal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Life After Music

podcast.title: Decline (Late 90s)
podcast.body: Britpop "crashed and burned" in a haze of cocaine and heroin, coinciding with the rise of electronica and a resurrection of British club culture. "And then that crashed and burned in a haze of cocaine and heroin."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 500th Show!

podcast.title: Defining Elements
podcast.body: Two key elements that defined the sound of Britpop, particularly as solidified by Blur's "Modern Life Is Rubbish," were the distinctive guitar work (exemplified by Graham Coxon) and lyrical content rich in British themes and exaltation of the United Kingdom (as written by Damon Albarn).

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: BLUR: Pilares del Brit Pop

podcast.title: Distraction from Bosnia Conflict
podcast.body: Britpop, particularly the media's focus on the rivalry between Oasis and Blur, served as a significant distraction for the British media from larger European issues, such as the growing problems in Bosnia. "Even though much of Europe's attention was focused on the growing problems in Bosnia, much of the British media spent their time chronicling the battle between Oasis and Blur."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Dominance in the Mid-90s
podcast.body: Britpop "ruled the day" in the post-grunge world, particularly around the time of Radiohead's "The Bends" album, creating a context where other sounds, like Radiohead's, initially struggled to catch on. The genre was characterized by rivalries like "Blur versus Oasis," and included bands like "Alaska" (likely a typo for Elastica) and "Pulp." "Britpop ruled the day. I mean, it was blur versus oasis. We had Alaska and pulp."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Radiohead - A History: Part 2

podcast.title: Dominant in Early 90s Britain
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, while PJ Harvey stood out as an individual artist, the rest of Britain was largely focused on the Britpop movement, following the Manchester Sound. "Well the rest of the country was about the Manchester Sound and then Brickpop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Women Who Rocked The 90's

podcast.title: Dreampop Integration
podcast.body: Dreampop significantly incorporated into the Britpop movement of the 1990s, indicating its deeper and more widespread legacy compared to shoegaze. "el dreampop se incorporó mucho a lo que seguía el britpop de los 90."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: DREAM POP y SHOEGAZE. Diferencias entre ellos.

podcast.title: Early 1990s Dominance
podcast.body: Britpop was an "awesome" and significant part of the early 1990s alternative rock landscape, alongside grunge, industrial, and Manchester scenes. Its prominence, however, waned by the late 1990s, reflecting a broader shift and search for the "next big thing" in rock music. "The awesomeness of the alternation of the early 1990s, with grunge and industrial and Manchester and Britpop, had faded away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

podcast.title: Early Nomenclature - "New Wave of New Wave"
podcast.body: Initially, the new music that would become Britpop was sometimes referred to as "the new wave of new wave," but this term was deemed too cumbersome. "at first people called this new music the new wave of new wave, but that was kind of a mouthful."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Emergence and Foundations
podcast.body: Britpop emerged after the decline of Madchester, building upon the foundations laid by the Manchester scene. "And then there's a bit of a law and then Brickpop comes along. But Brickpop's foundations were essentially Manchester."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Emergence and Impact in the 1990s
podcast.body: Britpop was an important and "amazing" part of the diverse music scene that flourished between 1991 and 1995. Its early development contributed to a period characterized by constant new sounds, songs, and scenes. "it was just, you know, the early part of Britpop, it was just amazing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence as a Record Product
podcast.body: The Britpop movement is often viewed and analyzed as a "record product," highlighting the strategic and commercial aspects of its development and popularization within the music industry.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: BLUR: Pilares del Brit Pop

podcast.title: Era in British History - Mid-90s
podcast.body: In the mid-90s, Britpop transcended music to become an entire era in British history, marked by a vibrant cultural, social, political, and economic atmosphere in London. It coincided with the rise of a young Prime Minister, Tony Blair, and a renewed sense of British pride among young people. "In the mid-90s, Britpop was more than just music. It was an era in British history."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Evolution from Manchester Movement
podcast.body: Britpop primarily evolved from the Manchester movement, with the early 1990s marking a transition point. Blur's first album, for instance, is seen by some as early Britpop and by others as late Manchester, signifying the emergence of a new movement largely dominated by multinational corporations and mass consumption. "el ripop bebe de varias fuentes pero el principal movimiento de evolución viene del movimiento Manchester porque tenemos ahí a primera solos 90 esos discos que no sabemos muy bien en qué lado ubicarlo"

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Sonido MADCHESTER

podcast.title: Foundation in The Smiths' Legacy
podcast.body: The Smiths' innovative approach to lyric writing and their new understanding of pop music are recognized as the significant foundation upon which the Britpop movement of the 1990s was built. "fue el gran cimiento sobre el que se basó la música del ripop de los 90."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: THE SMITHS: Un antes y un después en la forma de componer.

podcast.title: Golden Age and Early Gestation
podcast.body: The golden age of Britpop is generally considered to be between 1994 and 1996, but the movement, as a discographic product, began to take shape much earlier, in the very early 1990s. "la época dorada del Brypok fue entre el 94 y el 96 yo creo, el movimiento discográfico del Brypok se empezó a gestar mucho antes, ya muy primero se los 90."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El BRIT POP como negocio discográfico

podcast.title: Heterogeneous Nature
podcast.body: Britpop, as a musical movement, was very heterogeneous, encompassing many bands with widely dispersed styles. Despite this diversity, four major pillars (Blur, Oasis, Suede, and Pulp) were identified as defining and leading the movement.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: BLUR: Pilares del Brit Pop

podcast.title: Indie Label Submissions
podcast.body: The new wave of young bands forming the Britpop movement actively began sending their demo tapes to independent labels, indicating the genre's initial roots in the indie scene. "this new crop of young bands began sending demo tapes to independent labels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Indie Rock: Part 4

podcast.title: Indie-Driven Scene (Mid-90s)
podcast.body: The Britpop scene of the mid-1990s was nearly 100% indie-driven. Bands like Blur, on the small Food label, and Oasis, signed to the "formerly has been" Creation label, achieved massive success, transforming Britain's musical landscape as their "alternative" sounds became mainstream. "The brick pop scene was nearly 100% indie driven back in the middle of the 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Definition (from the vault)

podcast.title: Influence on British Indie Rock
podcast.body: Just as grunge significantly impacted North American guitar rock, Britpop had "long lasting influences on indie rock and Britain." "Just as Grunge has had long lasting influences on North American guitar rock, so has Britpop on indie rock and Britain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 3: Grunge

podcast.title: Influences and Origins
podcast.body: Britpop emerged as the next significant scene, drawing inspiration equally from the Madchester sound and esteemed British bands of the past, such as The Beatles, The Kinks, and The Mods. "Inspired equally by Manchester and great British bands of the past, like The Beatles and The Kings and the Mods, this new crop of young bands began sending demo tapes to independent labels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Indie Rock: Part 4

podcast.title: Integration with Electronic Music
podcast.body: The Chemical Brothers integrated quickly into the Britpop scene, forming friendships and collaborations with key figures, marking a novel fusion between electronic music and the dominant British rock culture of the 90s. "gente que se metió muy rápido dentro de la cultura rock y de la cultura indie y del Britpop británica."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: The Chemical Brothers. Padres de la cultura BIG BEAT

podcast.title: Intimate Listening Experience
podcast.body: Britpop, a significant genre of the 1990s, offered a more intimate and personal listening experience, typically enjoyed alone in one's room. This contrasted sharply with Eurodance, which was designed for communal dancing and shared revelry. "Ha diferenciado otras músicas de los 90 que eran más íntimas para escupir en la solidad de tu habitación, como el Brindpock..."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La gran mentira detrás del Eurodance

podcast.title: Lingering Influence
podcast.body: Despite its end, Britpop's influence continues to live on alongside its myths, legends, and stories. "Its influence would live along with all the myths and legends and stories, but all things must pass, you know."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 4: Britpop

podcast.title: Lingering Influence
podcast.body: Remnants of 90s Britpop were still evident in Noel Gallagher's solo albums, distinguishing them from Lee Amgala Gheri's newer work, which largely sheds these echoes. "tenían ese deje a lo mejor a restos de ripop de los 90."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Liam Gallagher - As you were (información y reseña)

podcast.title: Lodger's Delayed Influence
podcast.body: David Bowie's *Lodger* became an important influence for the Britpop movement and associated "match" (Madchester-like) sound from the late 1980s to the mid-1990s, with artists like Noel Gallagher and Brett Anderson referencing it. This influence emerged with a delay of 12-15 years after its release. "este Alban se convirtió en una importante influencia del pop británico, casi desde ese finales de los 80 a mediados de los 90 fue una pieza importante para definir el pop británico."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 3

podcast.title: Madchester Foundations
podcast.body: The foundations of Britpop were "essentially Madchester," indicating a direct lineage and influence from the earlier scene. "But Brickpop's foundations were essentially Madchester."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of "Madchester" - Part 2

podcast.title: Mainstream Thrust for Indie Bands
podcast.body: Britpop played a significant role in propelling indie bands into the mainstream across the UK, following the deep entrenchment of indie culture in the 1990s, particularly the Manchester scene. "Then came Britpuff which really thrust indie bands into the mainstream."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rock Snob

podcast.title: Major Label Strategies
podcast.body: Britpop emerged from crucial discographic strategies and a massive bet by many multinational corporations, which ultimately led to the movement's development. "detrás del Brypok hubo unas estrategias discográficas importantísimas y un enorme apuesta por muchas multinacionales que degeneraron en el movimiento."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El BRIT POP como negocio discográfico

podcast.title: Mid-1990s Growing Prominence
podcast.body: Originating from the United Kingdom and led by bands such as Blur and Oasis, Britpop was increasingly making its presence known in the mid-1990s, alongside the dominant grunge sound. "Aunque el Britpop, proveniente del reino unido y encabezado por bandas como Blue, Río Asis, estaba haciendo se notar cada vez más."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Por qué el cine de los 2000 sonaba así? Big Beat

podcast.title: Orchestrated Discographic Product
podcast.body: Contrary to a common idealized perception of independence, Britpop was fundamentally an "enormous discographic product" or a "discographic orgy" that was intentionally engineered by major record labels. "detrás del Brypok nos guste o no hubo un enorme producto discográfico, o sea el Brypok fue una orgía discográfica en contra de lo que muchas veces pensamos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El BRIT POP como negocio discográfico

podcast.title: Origin as Defense against Grunge
podcast.body: Britpop emerged in the early to mid-1990s as a "made in Britain approach" by young musicians to fight back against the perceived "musical imperialism" of grunge and American alt-rock, which threatened to "swamp" the UK music scene. "They decided to fight back with a real, made in Britain approach."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 4: Britpop

podcast.title: Origin of the Term "Britpop"
podcast.body: The term "Britpop" first appeared in *The Face* magazine's May 1994 issue during an interview with Blur, as an abbreviation of "British Pop" to describe the band's vision for a renewed emphasis on UK popular music. The *Guardian* newspaper then used the term, and it became widely adopted after an *NME* issue in January 1995. "The first appearance of the word seems to have been in the face... There was an interview with Blur in the May 1994 issue... The magazine then abbreviated that to Brit Pop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Overshadowing Dreampop (1990s)
podcast.body: Britpop (transcribed as "Redpop") is mentioned as a genre that emerged in the 1990s and contributed to Dreampop being overshadowed and moving to the margins.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Dreampop - A History

podcast.title: Post-Diana Decline
podcast.body: After the death of Princess Diana on August 31, 1997, the "wind was taken out of everybody's sales" for Britpop, contributing to its decline. "Then after Prince's Diana died on August 31, 1997, that really took the wind out of everybody's sales."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 9: The Festivals

podcast.title: Post-Rave/Shoegaze Void
podcast.body: The decline of 1980s club and rave culture, the end of the Madchester scene, and the failure of shoegaze to ignite the masses created a "big void in British music" which Britpop rushed to fill, aided by a desperate British music press. "Following the decline of the club and rave culture of the 1980s, there was this big void in British music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 4: Britpop

podcast.title: Presence in Early 1990s
podcast.body: Britpop was noted as one of the prominent music genres emerging or thriving in the early 1990s. "We got Britpop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rage Against The Machine: Part 2

podcast.title: Reasons for Decline
podcast.body: Several factors contributed to Britpop's decline from 1995-1996: a loss of focus with indie labels signing many subpar bands, widespread overexposure of major acts like Oasis (extending to personal lives like Noel Gallagher's wife Meg Matthews), the pressure on major bands to follow up monumental albums like *The Great Escape* and *Morning Glory*, and rampant drug use (heroin and cocaine) taking a toll on musicians and the industry. "First of all, everyone was starting to lose focus... Second, everyone else was being criminally overexposed... And third, it was soon time for the major players to release new albums... And fourth... was all that heroin and cocaine that was messing everybody's minds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Response to Grunge
podcast.body: Britpop emerged in the middle 1990s as a "nationalistic celebration of British music heritage," largely prompted by concerns in the UK over the rising popularity of American grunge bands, which was seen as coming "at the expensive homegrown British artists." "Consider the Britpop scene in the middle 1990s. That sound, that nationalistic celebration of British music heritage, was prompted in large part by grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 3: Grunge

podcast.title: Resurgence of Guitars
podcast.body: By the time the future members of the Arctic Monkeys became musically aware, Britpop was a dominant force, instrumental in bringing guitars back to the forefront of music.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Deconstructing the Arctic Monkeys

podcast.title: Rise in the 1990s
podcast.body: Britpop emerged as a new genre that dominated the 1990s. Following the acquisition of Creation Records by Sony, the label signed unknown bands like Oasis, who quickly became leaders of this movement. Oasis's second album, "(What's the Story) Morning Glory?", became the best-selling British album of the decade, exemplifying the genre's massive commercial success. "El Britpop, eso segundo álbum, Watch the Story, Modern Glory, se convirtió en el disco británico más vendido de la década."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El disco imposible: La historia de Loveless y My Bloody Valentine

podcast.title: Speaker's Fandom
podcast.body: The speaker is a self-professed "big Brit Pop fan." "I'm a big Brit Pop fan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Successor to Madchester
podcast.body: Britpop emerged after the decline of Madchester, following a brief lull in the British music scene. "And then there's a bit of a law and then Brickpop comes along."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of "Madchester" - Part 2

podcast.title: Term Coined in British Press
podcast.body: The word "Britpop" first appeared in the May 1994 issue of *The Face* magazine, following an interview with Blur discussing a renewed emphasis on British pop. It was then used by *The Guardian* and gained widespread adoption after an *NME* issue in January 1995. "The first appearance of the word seems to have been in the face, one of those new British magazines that I mentioned earlier."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 4: Britpop

podcast.title: The Bends' Influence on Britpop's Evolution
podcast.body: Radiohead's album *The Bends*, released in the mid-1990s as the golden era of Britpop was ending, played a curious role in pushing the genre towards more alternative or experimental sounds. Damon Albarn of Blur specifically cited *The Bends* as influencing his band to abandon classic Britpop for new sounds on their 1997 self-titled album. "posiblemente fue uno de los álbumes que ayudó al Britpop a empujarlo hacia otros nuevos lugares un poco más alternativos o más experimentales."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: RADIOHEAD: THE BENDS desde otra perspectiva

podcast.title: The British Invasion That Didn't Take
podcast.body: The 1990s Britpop era was largely immune to America, meaning "there was no 90s British invasion." Despite its own catalog of styles and stars, it serves as a "control group" in the multi-decade pop experiment, representing a British invasion that failed to cross over successfully to the US. "But here's the thing, America proved largely immune to that Britpop era. There was no 90s British invasion, which begs the question, why?"

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: The British Are Charting Edition Part 2

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: The British Are Charting Edition Part 2

podcast.title: The Good Mixer Pub as a Britpop Hub
podcast.body: In the early and middle 1990s, The Good Mixer pub on Inverness Street in Camden, London, became a crucial hangout spot for many individuals who would go on to form prominent Britpop bands. Musicians from groups like Blur, Oasis, The Libertines, The Darkness, and Travis were regulars. This establishment was a place where many bands were formed and songs took shape. Its popularity as a Britpop hub eventually led to an influx of fans, much to the chagrin of the original working-class clientele. "In the early and middle 90s, this became a hangout for many of the people who would form the bands of the era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Shrines ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: The Smiths' Foundation
podcast.body: The Smiths are credited with laying the foundations for Britpop, a genre that emerged a few years after their breakup and went on to dominate British pop music for nearly an entire decade. "it also laid the foundations for what would become Britpop a few years later."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

podcast.title: Think Tank's Departure from Britpop
podcast.body: While Blur's Think Tank aimed for commercial accessibility, it did not intend to be a return to their Britpop roots. "No pretendía volver al grip-pop, pero sí por lo menos hacer algo más accesible."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Blur - Think Tank y su dificil grabación.

podcast.title: Toronto as a Staging Ground for British Acts
podcast.body: Toronto served as a key staging ground for British bands breaking into the North American market, forming a "third leg of a triangle" with New York and London. Many British bands from 1984 credit the radio station for their success in North America. "Toronto is like the third leg of a triangle that extends through New York and London and a lot of British acts used to break into America by using Toronto as a staging ground."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Toronto's Role in North American Breakout
podcast.body: Toronto played a crucial role as a "staging ground" for many British acts from 1984 onwards to break into the North American market, forming a "third leg of a triangle that extends through New York and London." This support for British music meant Toronto-based radio stations often led the culture in promoting bands like Happy Mondays, Stone Roses, and The Charlatans, weeks ahead of other Canadian outlets and even US markets. "We did very well promoting British music because Toronto is like the third leg of a triangle that extends through New York and London."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: UK Alt Rock Contribution
podcast.body: Britpop is identified as the UK's primary contribution to Alt Rock during the 1990s. "if the UK's was Britpop, ours was Can Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 8: The CanRock Revolution
